newsitem.title: UK: Sell long-dated Treasuries, buy JGBs - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Sell long-dated Treasuries, buy JGBs - analysts.

text.p: Japanese and overseas investors may consider trading in their U.S. Treasuries for Japanese government bonds (JGBs), with the prospect of higher official interest rates in both markets, analysts said on Tuesday.
"Japanese investors could go back into Japan when the (bond) yield reaches 2.75 percent or three percent," said Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International in London.
"Overseas investors should be attracted into yen holdings if the dollar falls further," he added.
The dollar fell more than three yen on Tuesday, to below 112 yen, after reports that the ruling Liberal Democratic Party would recommend a rise in Japan's official discount rate.
An LDP source said later there had been no decision yet on whether to recommend raising the key rate, but added there were calls to the party to do so.
Comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin that a sustained increase in Japan's current account surplus would be a "serious problem" also contributed to the greenback's decline.
Meanwhile, global bond markets are on tenterhooks in advance of Tuesday's U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, which may lead to a rise in official U.S. interest rates.

U.S. and Japanese bonds were little moved by the dollar's fall. The U.S. 10-year note was quoted at 99-12 at 1130 GMT, to yield 6.712 percent, while the benchmark 182nd JGB was yielding 2.475 percent.
"The U.S./JGB spread will remain relatively unchanged in a small downward price trend short-term," said Shah.
"Longer term, the spread can widen to test the year's high of 500 basis points."
The 10-year spread was quoted at 414 basis points at 1130 GMT.
The market is divided as to whether the FOMC will act on rates on Tuesday.

Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International Europe in London, said the Fed would hold off until its next policy-setting meeting in July, while the Bank of Japan would wait until later in the year before raising rates.
"Just because the Fed raises rates in July, it does not mean the Bank of Japan will raise in July."
Shah, meanwhile, thought the U.S. would raise rates on Tuesday, and Japan would wait until the third quarter.
U.S. Treasury yields will rise to 6.95 percent at 30 years if the U.S. does act on Tuesday, Shah said, against their current 6.91 percent.
Japanese investors could stick with U.S. Treasuries but move to the shorter end of the curve, until JGB yields rise enough to entice them back home, Shah added.
Overseas investors, meanwhile, have already increased their exposure to yen cash and Euroyen holdings, analysts said, putting them in a good position to buy yen-denominated bonds.
Foreign investors' net purchases of yen bonds in April totalled a record high 5.1777 trillion yen, the Japan Securities Dealers' Association (JSDA) said on Tuesday.
Andrew Davies, bond analyst at London Bond Broking, saw a stronger yen benefiting Japanese stocks, rather than bonds.
"The Japanese stock market is looking in better shape. We could see portfolio investment into Japanese stocks."
A Reuters monthly global asset allocation survey of mostly UK-based fund managers on Monday showed an increased underweight position in U.S. equities, with Japan and cash the main beneficiaries.
